metadata.title: Students’ 2018 PISA reading self-concept: Identifying predictors and examining model generalizability for emergent bilinguals

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the 2018 PISA reading assessment for the United States and analyzes students nested within schools using multilevel modeling. The authors explicitly state that student sampling weights (scaled) were included in each analysis, and that replication weights were included in the multilevel models to account for between-cluster variance (e.g., schools) as recommended by the PISA manual and analytical framework. The analytic sample is restricted to the PISA 2018 reading assessment participants in the U.S. (N=4838 students) and further reduced through variable screening (excluding predictors with >20% missingness) and subsequent imputation steps. Because the paper does not report the exact weight variable name(s), the weighting strategy is documented at the methodological level (sampling weights + replication weights) rather than by a specific W_ variable code.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is students’ reading self-concept measured via a short Likert-style scale (three items) rather than a cognitive achievement score generated with PISA plausible values. Therefore, plausible values handling is not applicable to the outcome model. For missing data, the authors report a two-stage imputation strategy (PMM after a 20% missingness variable cutoff, then two-level fully conditional specification imputation for multilevel analyses), so the missing-data handling is documented rather than omitted.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the 2018 PISA reading assessment data for the United States. The analytic sample includes 4838 adolescents who participated in the PISA 2018 reading assessment. For variable inclusion, the authors applied a 20% missingness cutoff to exclude predictors with missing data rates beyond 20%, then imputed missing values for the remaining variables (PMM for ENET stage; two-level fully conditional specification for multilevel modeling). Teacher and school variables were aggregated to the school level because PISA does not provide student–teacher linkages.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Elastic Net variable selection (standardized coefficients in Tables 1-3); multilevel modeling (MLM) parameter estimates in Table 5. Significant predictors in full model: Reading habits (β=0.204, SE=0.014, p<0.001), Perceived ICT competence (β=0.153, SE=0.016, p<0.001), Work mastery (β=0.102, SE=0.016, p<0.001), Teacher understanding (β=0.089, SE=0.017, p<0.001), Attitude towards school (β=0.045, SE=0.017, p=0.009), Subjective well-being (β=-0.050, SE=0.016, p=0.002), Availability/usage of ICT (β=-0.081, SE=0.025, p=0.001), Competitiveness (β=0.072, SE=0.015, p<0.001), Father’s education (β=0.061, SE=0.010, p<0.001). School-level significant predictors: Hosting visiting teachers from other countries (β=-0.136, SE=0.042, p=0.001), Percentage disadvantaged homes (β=-0.003, SE=0.001, p=0.001), Percentage total funding from government (β=0.002, SE=0.001, p=0.038), School’s equity-oriented policies (β=0.055, SE=0.017, p=0.002). Model fit: LRT p<0.001; L1 R²=0.14 and L2 R²=0.16 in Table 5 (Model 3).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (United States; 15-year-olds) the study leveraged reading habits, perceived ICT competence, work mastery, teacher understanding, and subjective well-being to predict reading self-concept, finding that reading habits, ICT competence, work mastery, and teacher understanding were positive predictors while ICT availability/usage and subjective well-being were negative. This indicates that strengthening instructionally manipulable supports—especially reading engagement, mastery-oriented persistence, and teacher understanding—may improve reading self-concept, though the results are correlational and not causal.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (United States; emergent bilinguals vs native English speakers; 15-year-olds)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel modeling in Table 6. Emergent bilinguals (N=736): significant student-level predictors—Perceived ICT competence (β=0.150, SE=0.017, p<0.001), Work mastery (β=0.102, SE=0.018, p=0.004), Teacher understanding (β=0.087, SE=0.018, p=0.020), Reading habits (β=0.072, SE=0.036, p=0.049). Significant teacher-level predictor: Physical education in teacher training (β=-0.321, SE=0.145, p=0.030). Significant school-level predictors: Activities offered by school (β=-0.041, SE=0.018, p=0.026), Hosting visiting teachers from other countries (β=-0.088, SE=0.040, p=0.590 not significant per text), and others reported as non-significant for emergent bilinguals in the narrative; native English speakers (N=4054): significant student-level predictors include Availability/usage of ICT (β=-0.100, SE=0.028, p<0.001), Teacher understanding (β=0.089, SE=0.02, p<0.001), Work mastery (β=0.10, SE=0.02, p<0.001), Perceived ICT competence (β=0.15, SE=0.02, p<0.001), Reading habits (β=0.24, SE=0.02, p<0.001), Father’s education (β=0.054, SE=0.013, p<0.001). School-level significant for native English speakers: Activities offered by school (β=-0.04, SE=0.02, p=0.026), Hosting visiting teachers from other countries (β=-0.09, SE=0.04, p=0.032), Percentage disadvantaged homes (β=0.00, SE=0.00, p=0.052), Percentage total funding from government (β=0.00, SE=0.00, p=0.014). ICCs: emergent bilinguals show much higher between-school variance (adjusted ICC=0.10) than native English speakers (adjusted ICC=0.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (United States; emergent bilinguals vs native English speakers) the study leveraged perceived ICT competence, work mastery, reading habits, teacher understanding, and school-level equity-oriented context to predict reading self-concept, finding that the predictor set differs by home language: emergent bilinguals’ reading self-concept is more strongly associated with mastery, ICT competence, and teacher understanding, while native English speakers show additional associations with competitiveness, father’s education, and several school-level resource indicators. This indicates that one-size-fits-all models may miss subgroup-specific levers, so policies and school practices should tailor supports for emergent bilinguals around mastery-oriented persistence, teacher understanding, and ICT competence development.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 Reading data from the United States (N=4838 students aged ~15) to model reading self-concept, measured by three self-report items (“I am a good reader,” “I am able to understand difficult texts,” “I read fluently”). The authors first apply Elastic Net as a variable-selection machine-learning approach (R packages caret and glmnet) to identify salient predictors across student, teacher, and school levels, then estimate two-level multilevel models with replication weights to test statistical contributions and generalizability for emergent bilinguals (N=736) versus native English speakers (N=4054). In the full U.S. model, reading habits, perceived ICT competence, work mastery, and teacher understanding are positive predictors, while ICT availability/usage and subjective well-being are negative; school-level effects include government funding (+) and visiting teachers from other countries (−). The paper is correlational (not causal) and relies on composite-variable construction (CFA/PCA), so interpretation should focus on actionable associations rather than causal effects.
